clue.text: Select Scottish port for a Dickensian character

parts.note: Wick is a fishing port in Caithness, in the far north of Scotland

explanation.surface: Someone chooses a harbour in Scotland as a home for a character from Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Pickwick is the title figure of Dickens's novel The Pickwick Papers.

clue.text: Take advice by which the waiter might profit

definitions.text: by which the waiter might profit

explanation.surface: A waiter is counselled on how to earn more money.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: gathering useful hints, and literally collecting gratuities, as a waiter does from customers.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather hints is to learn from guidance; gratuities left on a table are the money a waiter gains.

clue.text: Soundly sequential at the breakfast table

definitions.note: a description, not a noun: the thing found on the breakfast table

indicators.note: 'soundly' says the word for 'sequential' is to be said out loud and spelt differently

parts.note: sequential means serial, one after another

explanation.surface: A tidy, orderly routine being followed over the morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: SERIAL and CEREAL sound alike; the definition names the cornflakes or porridge served at breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornflakes and other grain-based foods are the standard morning dish served in a bowl.

clue.text: Convoluted type of injury

explanation.surface: Someone describes a complicated sort of hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense rhymes with 'round': coiled or twisted, the past tense of wind. The second rhymes with 'tuned': a cut or gash.
explanation.definitionFit: Convoluted means coiled or twisted round, as a spring is; a cut or gash is a kind of bodily harm.

clue.text: As no cry is set up they make their mark

indicators.note: letters that are set up are arranged afresh, so the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Children who make no fuss once settled with their drawing materials leave marks everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' is the anagram signal on AS NO CRY; 'is' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Wax drawing sticks leave coloured lines on paper, which is how a child makes a mark.

clue.text: The spirit of Holland conventionally chosen in Switzerland

explanation.surface: A Dutch drink is picked, as tradition dictates, in the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: Geneva is an old name for Dutch gin (from French genièvre, juniper); the Swiss city is where the Geneva Conventions were agreed, hence 'conventionally'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch gin was once sold under this name, and the Swiss city hosted the treaties on wartime conduct.

clue.text: White bloomers enhance Alpine beauty

parts.note: 'bloomers' suggests underwear, but means flowers: a white-flowering mountain plant that adorns the Alps

explanation.surface: White knickers making a mountain girl even prettier.
explanation.definitionFit: This small white-flowered plant grows high in the Alps and is a national emblem of Switzerland and Austria.

clue.text: Curled up together we intend to be disentangled

indicators.note: something disentangled has its strands sorted out differently, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A couple wrapped round each other plan to separate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be disentangled' is the anagram signal on WE INTEND, a nice contrast with the definition's tangle.
explanation.definitionFit: Things twisted round one another, like vines or ropes, are interwoven.

clue.text: Apprehended when checked

explanation.surface: Someone was caught when their progress was halted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' only links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Police apprehend a suspect by taking them into custody; checked progress is halted or stopped.

clue.text: ! A round robin perhaps?

parts.note: a round robin is not a bird here but a message copied to many people at once

explanation.surface: Musing on whether a plump little bird is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The '!' before the clue is a stray mark on the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: A round robin is a single message duplicated and sent to a whole list of recipients.

clue.text: See 9
The poker player's stake in neat disarray

indicators.note: something in disarray is jumbled, so the letters of the word before are mixed up
something in disarray is jumbled, so the letters of the word before are mixed up

explanation.surface: A gambler's chips are piled untidily on the table.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker, each player puts a fixed sum into the pot before the deal.

clue.text: To and fro in every direction especially vertically

explanation.surface: Someone describes movement back and forth all over the place.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means back and forth (pacing it), and literally rising and falling.
explanation.definitionFit: Pacing back and forth is moving this way; rising and falling is motion along the vertical.

clue.text: Attends upon Christmas singers

explanation.surface: Someone serves carollers at the festive season.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the 'waits' were bands of carol singers going door to door at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: A servant attends upon a master, as a waiter serves diners; the festive carollers were traditionally called by this old name.

clue.text: Resistance units initially heading many an official communication

definitions.text: initially heading many an official communication

explanation.surface: Electrical units appear at the top of government letters.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, official letters are stamped O.H.M.S., the initials of On His Majesty's Service; the ohm is the unit of electrical resistance.
explanation.definitionFit: The unit of electrical resistance is named after Georg Ohm; the initials of On His Majesty's Service head government mail.

clue.text: Posh, though perhaps shrill

explanation.surface: An upper-class voice that may also be piercing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'though perhaps' only links the two senses: superior in manner, and high-pitched.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone posh affects superior manners; a shrill sound is pitched high.

clue.text: By no means a good-looker, and superstitiously malignant

explanation.surface: Someone is described as plain and believed to bring bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good-looker' is read literally: a gaze that does harm, the curse believed to come from a malevolent stare.
explanation.definitionFit: Folk belief holds that a malevolent glance can bring misfortune; such a glance is no kindly looker.

clue.text: See 1
Refreshment for the novice golfer, we hear?

indicators.note: 'we hear' says the words for 'novice golfer' are to be spoken and spelt another way

parts.note: a novice is green, and a golfer drives off from a tee

explanation.surface: A drink for a beginner on the links.
explanation.walkthrough: GREEN TEE sounds the same as the Chinese drink; 'for the' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfermented leaf brewed into a drink is a light thirst-quencher.

clue.text: Searches for food for a long time

explanation.surface: An animal hunts for something to eat for an age.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that hunt about for something to eat are gathering provisions.

clue.text: Wine to plunder

explanation.surface: Drink taken as loot.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is an old name for sherry-like white wine from Spain, as in Falstaff's sack.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortified Spanish white wine was called sack; to sack a city is to pillage it.

clue.text: He girl to avoid

explanation.surface: Advice about a young woman best kept away from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' only links the two senses: an unmarried young woman, and to fail to hit.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried young woman is addressed by this title; to escape or fail to hit something is to dodge it.

clue.text: Ascertain extent of an old dance

explanation.surface: Someone sizes up a historical step.
explanation.walkthrough: A measure was a stately court dance of the sixteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: To find the size of something is to gauge it; a stately court dance of Tudor times bore this name.

clue.text: A term's recollection of running water

indicators.note: read as re-collection, the letters are gathered up again in a new order

explanation.surface: Memories of a school term spent beside a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recollection' looks like memory, but split as re-collection it is the anagram signal on A TERM'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A brook or small river is a flow of moving water.

clue.text: Comparatively little supported by something to be learnt

parts.note: less is the comparative of little
something on another is supported by it; in a down clue ON sits beneath LESS

explanation.surface: A small thing propped up by something you must study.
explanation.definitionFit: A teaching session or moral gives the pupil material to master.

clue.text: Wrench away what remains for the listener

indicators.note: 'for the listener' says the word for 'what remains' is to be heard, then spelt another way

explanation.surface: Someone tears off whatever is left over, as heard.
explanation.definitionFit: To twist or pull something forcibly from someone's grip is to snatch it.

clue.text: One-time royal apple-woman

explanation.surface: A former queen known for selling fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Charlotte was George III's wife; an apple charlotte is a baked pudding of fruit in buttered bread, so it is an 'apple' woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: George III's queen bore this name; it is also a woman's name given to a fruit pudding baked in bread.

clue.text: The cricketer's Upper House

explanation.surface: A cricket player's own parliamentary chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, home of the MCC; the House of Lords is the upper chamber of the UK Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous London cricket ground belongs to the game's players; peers sit in Parliament's upper chamber.

clue.text: Busily occupied mentally-on where to find the camper?

explanation.surface: Someone is lost in thought inside their canvas shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN TENT it says where a camper sleeps; whole, it means absorbed or concentrated.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone absorbed in a task is concentrating hard; a camper sleeps under canvas.

clue.text: Accommodation in four parts

explanation.surface: Lodgings divided four ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' only links: lodgings, and a whole cut into fourths.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodgings, especially soldiers' billets, are living rooms; a whole cut into four equal shares gives fourths.

clue.text: Semi-soft drink at the bar and in shy surroundings

indicators.note: one word sits in the other, the timid word forming the surroundings

explanation.surface: A bashful drinker orders something mild at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The container signal is split: 'in' and 'surroundings' frame the timid word. Shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, hence only half a soft drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer topped up with lemonade is half alcoholic, half fizzy pop.

clue.text: One of those men of Harlech no doubt

definitions.text: One of those men of Harlech no doubt

parts.words: One of those men of Harlech no doubt
parts.note: Harlech is a town in Gwynedd, and 'Men of Harlech' is a famous marching song from that country

explanation.surface: Thinking of a singer of a rousing old marching song.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlech is in north Wales, so its men are natives of that country.
